questions.q: Which describes the data science hiring process most accurately?
options: It is identical at every company
It has common building blocks, but rounds and order vary by employer
It consists only of a coding test
It never includes behavioral questions
questions.explain: Processes vary, but recruiter screens, SQL/coding, stats and ML, case work and behavioral questions recur.

questions.q: Junior data science roles frequently emphasize which areas?
options: Only advanced research mathematics
Only cloud architecture
SQL, statistics fundamentals and communication
Managing large teams
questions.explain: Employers often expect to teach advanced skills, so SQL, statistics basics and communication are commonly tested.

questions.q: What are the three beats of a strong 'tell me about yourself' answer?
options: Where you come from, what you built, what you want next
Your age, your hobbies, your salary
Every job you have ever had in order
Only your education
questions.explain: Background, a concrete project with a result, and your target role make a concise, useful pitch.

questions.q: How should you treat a job title such as 'Data Scientist' when preparing?
options: Assume it always means deep learning research
Assume it always means dashboards only
Ignore the posting entirely
Read the description, since titles are inconsistent across companies
questions.explain: The same title can mean analytics, machine learning or research work, so the description guides preparation.

questions.q: Which is a sensible attitude toward rejections during a job search?
options: They are common and not a verdict on you, so keep applying and practicing
Stop applying until you feel perfectly ready
Never ask for feedback
Assume you must restart your training
questions.explain: Rejections are common, especially early in a career; steady practice and applications matter.
